newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Somali faction plays down peace deal.
newsitem.headline: Somali faction plays down peace deal.

text.p: Somalia's latest peace accord looked in trouble on Thursday after the country's most powerful faction played it down while roadblocks remained in place in Mogadishu and factions clung to their positions.
The faction loyal to south Modagishu leader Hussein Aideed told a news conference in the Kenyan capital Nairobi on Thursday that faction leaders had merely agreed to continue dialogue in the future.
Jama Mohamed Ghalib, Aideed's foreign minister in his unrecognised government, said the key issue of Aideed's claim to the presidency was also not negotiable.
"Under guidance of Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi, Somali leaders have reached some understanding. The understanding is that dialogue will continue and this will lead to other things," Ghalib said.
But he said Aideed's position -- key to resolving Somalia's impasse as other factions dispute his role as president -- was not an issue for bargaining.
"The position of our presidency is not negotiable now or in the future. He is president of Somalia," Ghalib added.

A statement issued by the Kenyan government on Tuesday said factions leaders Hussein, Ali Mahdi of north Mogadishu and his ally Osman Atto had signed a peace agreement. The accord included end to hostilities, removal of road blocks in the country and free movement of people.
But in the divided city Mogadishu roadblocks remained in place and rival militia forces held their positions as the city awaited the return of faction leaders from talks in Kenya.
Somali sources said on Thursday faction members were waiting to hear details on how to implement the agreement which former colonial power Italy hailed as a breakthrough.
It was not known when the faction leaders -- Hussein Aideed, Ali Mahdi Mohamed and Ali Hassan Osman Atto -- would return to Somalia from the Kenyan capital.
"We have heard everything, now we must be told by the leadership what we should exactly do," said Ali Abdul, a militiaman loyal to Hussein Aideed in south Mogadishu.
Analysts in Mogadishu said the peace deal was certainly headed for the graveyard if Aideed refused to renounce his claim to the presidency. Ali Mahdi also calls himself president of Somalia.

The agreement had not immediately changed anything on the ground in Mogadishu, which remained divided into the northern stronghold of Ali Mahdi and the southern region held by Aideed, with Atto in between.
"The roadblocks are still around and there haven't been any celebrations yet. People are still awaiting the return of the leaders. We will see how it goes," said one resident.
The agreement, one of many signed by Somali factions since the country disintegrated after the 1991 overthrow of dictator Mohamed Siad Barre, was announced late on Tuesday after a week of contacts.
Under the agreement, the factions also agreed to facilitate delivery of humanitarian aid to Somalis and pledged continued dialogue among themselves.

Officials said the three faction heads had met face-to-face three times. Somali sources said it was the first direct meeting between Ali Mahdi and Aideed, a 34-year-old former U.S. marine who took over from his father Mohamed Farah Aideed following his death in Mogadishu on August 1.
Aideed, like his father, was elected president of Somalia by supporters and heads a government recognised only by Libya and Sudan.
